facts.statement: Physornis was scientifically described by Florentino Ameghino in 1895.
facts.quote: authority: Ameghino, 1895

facts.statement: Physornis fossils date from the Oligocene to the Miocene epochs.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Paleogene-Neogene (Oligocene-Miocene)

facts.statement: Physornis lived during the Oligocene epoch in what is now Argentina.
facts.quote: lived during the Oligocene epoch of the Paleogene in what is now Argentina

facts.statement: The species formerly known as P. brasiliensis is now classified in the genus Paraphysornis.
facts.quote: It is now in its own genus, Paraphysornis

facts.statement: Physornis is considered one of the largest known terror birds.
facts.quote: Physornis is among the largest phoursrhacids known

facts.statement: Based on relatives, Physornis may have reached a height of 2 meters at the head.
facts.quote: Based on its relatives, it may have been 2 m tall at the head

facts.statement: One preserved mandible specimen measured 15 cm in length.
facts.quote: Its mandible is wide, deep, and relatively large, with one specimen measuring 15 cm in preserved length

facts.statement: The tarsometatarsus was stocky with a large, flat dorsal surface.
facts.quote: The tarsometatarsus is similarly stocky, with a giant, flat dorsal (top) face

facts.statement: Physornis is one of two named physornithines, giant terror birds that lived in the Oligocene of South America.
facts.quote: It is one of two named physornithines, a group of giant phorusrhacids that lived in the Oligocene of South America

facts.statement: Fossils of Physornis have only been found in Deseadan deposits in Santa Cruz and Chubut Provinces.
facts.quote: Fossils of Physornis have exclusively been recovered from Deseadan deposits in Santa Cruz and Chubut Provinces

facts.statement: The first fossils were discovered in the Pyrotherium beds near Puerto Deseado in eastern Santa Cruz Province, Argentina.
facts.quote: Fossils assigned to Physornis were first discovered in the "Pyrotherium beds" of Puerto Deseado near the Deseado River, eastern Santa Cruz Province, Argentina

facts.statement: The initial discovery consisted of a single fossil fragment comprising the mandibular symphysis and part of the right mandible.
facts.quote: Only a single fossil, a fragment of the mandibular symphysis (the area where the mandibulae (lower jaws) meet) and attached portion of the right mandible, was found

facts.statement: In 1895, Ameghino named the new species Physornis fortis.
facts.quote: In 1895, Ameghino scientifically described the specimen and assigned it to a new genus and species of phorusrhacid bird, which he dubbed Physornis fortis

facts.statement: The genus name combines Greek roots meaning 'bellows' and 'bird'.
facts.quote: The generic name is a combination of the Greek roots φύσια (physero) meaning "bellows" and ὄρνις (ornis) meaning "bird"

facts.statement: The type specimen was sold to the Natural History Museum in London in 1895 or 1896.
facts.quote: This specimen was kept in Ameghino's personal collection until 1895 or 1896, when Ameghino sold it and several other Argentine bird fossils to the Natural History Museum, London

facts.statement: The type specimen is cataloged as BMNH-A583.
facts.quote: There, the specimen was deposited under catalog number BMNH-A583

facts.statement: An Amherst College expedition to Argentina's Sarmiento Formation began in 1911.
facts.quote: In 1911, Amherst College mounted an expedition to Sarmiento Formation deposits in Chubut Province, Argentina

facts.statement: The Field Museum launched expeditions to Argentina and Bolivia in 1922.
facts.quote: In 1922, the Field Museum launched the Captain Marshall Field Expeditions to fossiliferous outcrops in Argentina and Bolivia

facts.statement: Specimens discovered by Sternberg were later assigned to Physornis.
facts.quote: These specimens were later assigned to Physornis

facts.statement: In 1941, Bryan Patterson suggested the holotype might not be avian.
facts.quote: In 1941, American ornithologist Bryan Patterson stated that, after an in person examination, Physornis' holotype was likely not avian

facts.statement: Patterson speculated the holotype could be a fragment from a giant mammal like Parastrapotherium or Pyrotherium.
facts.quote: Instead, he speculated that it could be a shard from the iliac crest of a giant mammal like Parastrapotherium or Pyrotherium

facts.statement: Patterson provisionally classified the holotype as a nomen dubium.
facts.quote: He provisionally considered it a nomen dubium

facts.statement: Pierce Brodkorb argued in 1967 that the holotype was valid.
facts.quote: In contrast, studies like by American paleontologist Pierce Brodkorb (1967) argued that it was actually valid

facts.statement: A 2003 reexamination by Alvarenga and Höfling confirmed the holotype was valid but extremely fragmentary.
facts.quote: Upon reexamination, a 2003 article by Brazilian paleontologists Herculano Alvarenga and Elizabeth Höfling found that it was valid, although extremely fragmentary

facts.statement: Alvarenga and Höfling classified Physornis as a close relative of Paraphysornis and Brontornis, noting Brontornis is now a galliform.
facts.quote: They stated it was a close relative of the other phorusrhacids Paraphysornis and Brontornis, though the latter is now classified as a galliform

facts.statement: Brodkorb and other studies have considered Aucornis eurhynchus a synonym of P. fortis.
facts.quote: Due to similarities in their symphysis morphology, Brodkorb (1967) and several other studies have considered it a synonym of P. fortis

facts.statement: Alvarenga and Höfling classified Aucornis solidus as a species inquirenda in 2003 due to potential synonymy with Andrewsornis.
facts.quote: Although Brodkorb (1967) considered it a synonym of P. fortis, Alvarenga and Höfling (2003) opted to classify it as a species inquirenda because it could be a synonym of Andrewsornis as well

facts.statement: Federico Agnolín labeled Aucornis solidus as a nomen dubium in 2007.
facts.quote: However, in 2007 Argentine paleontologist Federico Agnolín labeled it a nomen dubium instead

facts.statement: Alvarenga concluded in 1993 that P. brasiliensis belongs to the genus Paraphysornis.
facts.quote: In 1993, Alvarenga came to the conclusion that it was actually its own genus, which he named Paraphysornis

facts.statement: The fragmentary nature of the fossils makes determining the size of Physornis difficult.
facts.quote: Due to its fragmentary, the size of Physornis is difficult to ascertain

facts.statement: Recent studies estimate Physornis was over 2 meters tall and similar in size to Brontornis.
facts.quote: However, more recent study by Alvarenga and Höfling estimated it to have been over 2 m tall and around the size of Brontornis

facts.statement: Brontornis was previously thought to measure up to 2.8 meters in height and weigh 350-400 kg.
facts.quote: At the time, Brontornis which was thought to have measured 2.8 m in maximum height and 350-400 kg in mass

facts.statement: Physornis had a stockier build with a shorter, thicker tarsometatarsus and a proportionally shorter, wider, and taller mandibular symphysis compared to other phorusrhacids.
facts.quote: Overall, it had a stockier, more giant build with a shorter, thicker tarsometatarsus and proportionally shorter, wider, and taller mandibular symphysis than other phorusrhacids

facts.statement: These physical traits are characteristic of the subfamily Physornithinae, which includes some of the largest phorusrhacids.
facts.quote: This is characteristic of Physornithinae, which features some of the largest members of the clade

facts.statement: Physornis has mandible branches that are further apart from the median, suggesting a wider skull base compared to Phorusrhacos.
facts.quote: In contrast to those of Phorusrhacos, the branches of the mandibles are further apart from the median and suggest that the skull has a wider base.

facts.statement: The mandibular symphysis of Physornis is constricted, wide, and has a flat ventral side.
facts.quote: The symphysis is constricted and wide with a flat ventral (bottom) side.

facts.statement: Individual variation exists in Physornis symphyses, with specimen FM-P13340 having a flat dorsal surface and FM-P13619 having a longitudinal channel.
facts.quote: Individual variation has been observed in the symphyses: specimen FM-P13340 bears a flat dorsal (top) symphyseal surface, meanwhile FM-P13619 has a longitudinal channel (a raised portion of bone) that runs the length of the bone.

facts.statement: The distal end of the Physornis femur is enlarged with flattened condyles.
facts.quote: The distal (away from body) end of the femur is enlarged with flattened condyles (shallow areas of articulation for other bones).

facts.statement: A giant, deep fossa is located on the posterior face of the Physornis femur above the condyles.
facts.quote: Above these condyles on the posterior face of the bone is a giant, deep fossa (a depression in bone).

facts.statement: The known part of the Physornis tarsometarsus is the proximal end, which features a quadrangular later cotyl and a short, widened dorsal face.
facts.quote: The tarsometarsus is only represented by the proximal end, though it displays unique traits such as a quadrangular later cotyl (an extension of bone that articulates with the condyles) and a short, widened dorsal face.

facts.statement: The lateral margin of the Physornis hipotarsus has a prominent crest on its posterior face, a trait not found in Brontornis or Paraphysornis.
facts.quote: The lateral margin of the hipotarsus (a bony process on the posterior side of the tarsometatarsus) has a prominent crest on its posterior (back) face, unlike in Brontornis and Paraphysornis.

facts.statement: Argentine paleontologist Federico Agnolín established the subfamily Physornithinae for Physornis and Paraphysornis in 2007.
facts.quote: In 2007 Argentine paleontologist Federico Agnolín erected the subfamily Physornithinae for Physornis and Paraphysornis.

facts.statement: Physornis shares characteristics with graviportal, large-bodied dromornithids and Gastornis.
facts.quote: These characteristics are comparable to those of the similarly graviportal (slow moving), large-bodied dromornithids and Gastornis.

facts.statement: Unlike the running genera Phorusrhacos, Procariama, and Psilopterus, Physornis was a graviportal ambush hunter.
facts.quote: Unlike the cursorial genera Phorusrhacos, Procariama, and Psilopterus, Physornis was a graviportal ambush hunter based on its proportions.

facts.statement: Brazilian researchers Herculano Alvarenga and Elizabeth Höfling discussed phorusrhacid habits in a 2003 article.
facts.quote: Brazilian researchers Herculano Alvarenga and Elizabeth Höfling made some general remarks about phorusrhacid habits in a 2003 article.

facts.statement: Physornis was flightless, evidenced by the proportional size of its wings and body mass, with wing size being more reduced in larger group members.
facts.quote: They were flightless, as evidenced by the proportional size of their wings and body mass, and wing-size was more reduced in larger members of the group.

facts.statement: Large lacrimal bone expansions above the eyes of Physornis suggest it hunted by sight in open, sunlit areas rather than shaded forests.
facts.quote: The large expansions above the eyes formed by the lacrimal bones (similar to what is seen in modern hawks) would have protected the eyes against the sun, and enabled keen eyesight, which indicates they hunted by sight in open, sunlit areas, and not shaded forests.

facts.statement: Dreyer and colleagues used ground-section microscopy on bone samples from the FM-P13619 limb bones to study Physornis growth.
facts.quote: Using the limb bones of FM-P13619, Dreyer and colleagues extracted thin bone samples which they studied using ground-section microscopy.

facts.statement: Physornis displayed a pattern of rapid growth similar to modern birds, indicated by a transition from vascularized to laminar bone tissue.
facts.quote: Both Andrewsornis and Physornis displayed a consistent pattern of rapid growth, similar to that of modern birds, shown by the transition of its fibrolamellar bone from greatly vascularized to less vascularized and more laminar.

facts.statement: Physornis fossils lacked lines of arrested growth (LAGs), indicating continuous bone growth without pauses.
facts.quote: Additionally, all fossils lacked LAGs (lines of arrested growth), indicating no pauses in the bone growth.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that cursoriality and graviportality exist on a spectrum, and Physornis may have been capable of short, fast bursts of speed.
facts.quote: Furthermore, the authors noted that cursoriality (adaptations for running) and graviportality (adaptations for slower movement) are on a spectrum, going on to state that Physornis could have conducted short, fast bursts sprints at times.
